source: Based on 'Electrical Apprenticeship Phase 4 Electrical Science Notes' (D. Ó Briain). Reworded; all answers recalculated to 3 d.p.

examples.title: Find the long side (hypotenuse)
examples.problem: A right-angled triangle has sides **20** and **15**. Find the **hypotenuse** and the angle θ next to the side of 20.
examples.tip: Remember **SOH CAH TOA**: Sin = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite ÷ Adjacent. In AC work this same triangle is the impedance triangle: Z is the hypotenuse, R is next to θ.

examples.title: Peak voltage to RMS
examples.problem: The mains has a **peak voltage** (V<sub>P</sub>) of **325 V**. Find the **RMS** voltage and the **peak-to-peak** voltage.
examples.tip: Going **from peak to RMS: × 0.707** (or ÷ √2). Going **from RMS to peak: ÷ 0.707** (or × √2). Using √2 on the calculator is more accurate than 0.707.

examples.title: Instantaneous value of a sine wave
examples.problem: A sine wave has a peak of **325 V**. What is the voltage at **45°** and at **270°**?
examples.tip: sin 0° = 0, sin 90° = 1, sin 180° = 0, sin 270° = −1, sin 360° = 0. Set the calculator to **degrees (D)**, not radians.

examples.title: Inductive reactance and current
examples.problem: A **0.3 H** inductor is on a **230 V, 50 Hz** supply. Find the **inductive reactance** X<sub>L</sub> and the current.
examples.tip: Higher frequency → **higher** X<sub>L</sub>. In an inductor the current **lags** the voltage by 90°.

examples.title: Capacitive reactance and current
examples.problem: A **1 mF** capacitor is on a **230 V, 50 Hz** supply. Find the **capacitive reactance** X<sub>C</sub> and the current.
examples.tip: Calculator: type **2 × π × 50 × 1 ×10ˣ −3**, press =, then press **x⁻¹** and =. Higher frequency → **lower** X<sub>C</sub>. In a capacitor the current **leads** the voltage by 90°.

examples.title: Resistor and inductor in series (R–L)
examples.problem: A coil has **R = 20 Ω** and **L = 0.3 H**. It is on **230 V, 50 Hz**. Find the **impedance**, the **current**, the **power factor** and the **phase angle**.
examples.tip: Inductive loads are **lagging** (I lags V).

examples.title: Resistor and capacitor in series (R–C)
examples.problem: **R = 20 Ω** is in series with **C = 100 μF** on **230 V, 50 Hz**. Find X<sub>C</sub>, Z and the current.
examples.tip: Capacitive loads are **leading** (I leads V).

examples.title: R, L and C all in series
examples.problem: **R = 20 Ω**, **L = 0.3 H** and **C = 100 μF** are in series on **230 V, 50 Hz**. Find Z and the current.
examples.tip: X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> pull in **opposite directions**, so **subtract** them before squaring.

examples.title: Resistor and capacitor in parallel (simple)
examples.problem: A capacitor takes **2 A** and a resistor in parallel with it takes **1.5 A**, on a 100 V, 50 Hz supply. Find the **supply current**.
steps: In parallel the currents are **not in phase**, so you cannot just add them
examples.tip: In parallel the **voltage** is the same across every branch. Work out each branch current first.

examples.title: Resistor and capacitor in parallel (with values)
examples.problem: A **45 μF** capacitor and a **70 Ω** resistor are in parallel on **110 V, 50 Hz**. Find the supply current.

examples.title: R, L and C in parallel: current, angle and power
examples.problem: **R = 10 Ω**, **X<sub>L</sub> = 12.5 Ω** and **X<sub>C</sub> = 20 Ω** are in parallel on **100 V, 50 Hz**. Find each branch current, the supply current, the phase angle and the power.
examples.tip: Power is only used by the **resistor**: 100 V × 10 A = 1000 W. That's a good way to check your answer.

examples.title: Time constant of a capacitor
examples.problem: A **1000 μF** capacitor charges through a **3 kΩ** resistor from a **9 V** supply. Find the **time constant**, the voltage after one time constant, and after 5 time constants.
steps: After 5τ (15.000 s) it reaches about **99 %**: 0.99 × 9 = **8.910 V** (treated as fully charged)
examples.tip: **63 % after 1τ, fully charged after 5τ.** k = 10³, μ = 10⁻⁶.

examples.title: Star-connected load: find X<sub>L</sub>
examples.problem: A balanced **star** load is on a **400 V** supply. Each phase has **R = 20 Ω** and an inductor. The line current is **9.2 A**. Find X<sub>L</sub> in each phase.
steps: Star: U<sub>P</sub> = U<sub>L</sub> ÷ √3 and I<sub>P</sub> = I<sub>L</sub>
Z² = R² + X<sub>L</sub>², so X<sub>L</sub>² = Z² − R²
examples.tip: If you round U<sub>P</sub> to 230 V early you get Z = 25 Ω and X<sub>L</sub> = 15 Ω. Keep the full number in the calculator for 3 decimal places.

examples.title: Delta-connected load: line current and PF
examples.problem: A balanced **delta** load is on a **400 V** supply. Each phase has **R = 20 Ω** and **X<sub>L</sub> = 15 Ω**. Find the line current and the power factor.
steps: Delta: U<sub>P</sub> = U<sub>L</sub> = 400 V and I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × I<sub>P</sub>
PF = cos θ = R ÷ Z = 20 ÷ 25 = **0.800 lagging**
examples.tip: **Star**: line voltage is √3 × phase voltage, currents equal. **Delta**: voltages equal, line current is √3 × phase current.

examples.title: Flux in an air-cored solenoid
examples.problem: An air-cored ring solenoid has a mean length of **0.2 m**, a cross-section of **1000 mm²**, **1000 turns** and carries **2 A**. Find the flux density B and the flux Φ.
examples.tip: mm² to m²: **× 10⁻⁶**. Flux Φ is in webers (Wb); flux density B is in tesla (T) = Wb/m².

examples.title: Current needed for a given flux
examples.problem: A solenoid of **10,000 turns** is wound on a ring with a mean diameter of **100 mm** and a cross-section of **0.01 m²**. What current gives a flux of **5 mWb**?
steps: Path length l = π × diameter = π × 0.1 = 0.314 m
H = (I × N) ÷ l, so I = (H × l) ÷ N

examples.title: Generator EMF when speed and flux change
examples.problem: A loop turns at **10 r/s** in a flux of **60 mWb** and makes **8 V**. Find the EMF at **16 r/s** with a flux of **50 mWb**.
steps: E is proportional to Φ × n, so E₂ ÷ E₁ = (Φ₂ ÷ Φ₁) × (n₂ ÷ n₁)
examples.tip: Put the **new** values on top and the **old** values underneath.

examples.title: Alternator frequency
examples.problem: An **8-pole** alternator runs at **750 r/min**. What frequency does it make?
steps: f = (p × N) ÷ 60, where p = **pairs** of poles and N = r/min
examples.tip: Always halve the number of poles to get **pole pairs**.

examples.title: Alternator poles and a new speed
examples.problem: An alternator at **20 r/s** gives **140 V at 60 Hz**. How many poles has it? What are the voltage and frequency at **32 r/s** (same flux)?
steps: f = p × n, so p = f ÷ n = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 pairs = **6 poles**
Flux is the same, so E is proportional to n: E₂ = 140 × (32 ÷ 20) = **224 V**

examples.title: Synchronous speed
examples.problem: A **4-pole** motor runs from a **50 Hz** supply. Find its **synchronous speed** in rpm.
examples.tip: Same answer as 120 × f ÷ poles = 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rpm.

examples.title: Percentage slip
examples.problem: A motor has a synchronous speed of **1500 rpm** and runs at **1450 rpm**. Find the **slip**.

examples.title: Rotor speed from slip
examples.problem: A **6-pole**, **50 Hz** motor has **8 % slip**. Find the rotor speed.
steps: 8 % slip means the rotor runs at 100 − 8 = **92 %** of N<sub>S</sub>
examples.tip: Quick way: rotor speed = N<sub>S</sub> × (100 − slip) ÷ 100.

examples.title: Find synchronous speed and poles from the rotor speed
examples.problem: An induction motor runs at **1470 rpm** with **3 % slip** on **50 Hz**. Find the synchronous speed and the number of poles.
steps: The rotor runs at 97 % of N<sub>S</sub>: 1470 = N<sub>S</sub> × 0.97
Pole pairs must be a whole number, so **2 pairs = 4 poles**
examples.tip: Real synchronous speeds on 50 Hz are 3000, 1500, 1000, 750 rpm… so the true N<sub>S</sub> here is 1500 rpm.

examples.title: Prefixes: mF and μF to farads
examples.problem: Write **1 mF**, **100 μF** and **45 μF** in farads.
examples.tip: On the calculator use the **×10ˣ** key: 45 ×10ˣ −6. It avoids counting zeros.

questions.q: A right-angled triangle has sides **6** and **8**. Find the **hypotenuse**.
The hypotenuse is **13** and one side is **5**. Find the **other side**.
In an impedance triangle **R = 30 Ω** and **Z = 50 Ω**. Find the angle **θ** (degrees).
In a right-angled triangle, **cos θ** equals…
questions.w: Remember **CAH**: Cos = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse.

questions.q: Which side is the **hypotenuse**?
o: The side next to the angle θ
The side opposite the angle θ
The longest side, opposite the right angle
questions.w: The hypotenuse is always the longest side and sits opposite the 90° angle.

questions.q: The RMS voltage is **230 V**. Find the **peak** voltage.
A sine wave has a peak of **340 V**. Find the **RMS** voltage.
A sine wave has a peak of **12 A**. Find the **average** value (over half a cycle).
A sine wave has a peak of **100 V**. What is the voltage at **30°**?
What is the frequency of the Irish mains supply?
questions.w: Mains is **50 Hz**: 50 complete cycles every second.

questions.q: **Peak-to-peak** voltage is…
questions.w: From the top of the wave to the bottom: V<sub>P</sub> + V<sub>P</sub> = 2 × V<sub>P</sub>.

questions.q: **47 μF** in farads is…
**2.2 kΩ** in ohms is…
**1 nF** is…
questions.w: n (nano) = 10⁻⁹.

questions.q: Which calculator key turns 2πfC into **1 ÷ 2πfC**?
questions.w: Work out 2πfC, then press **x⁻¹** and =. That gives the reciprocal.

questions.q: Find **X<sub>L</sub>** for a **0.15 H** inductor at **50 Hz**.
Find **X<sub>C</sub>** for a **47 μF** capacitor at **50 Hz**.
A **0.2 H** inductor is on **230 V, 50 Hz**. Find the **current**.
If the frequency goes **up**, inductive reactance X<sub>L</sub>…
questions.w: X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL: f is on top, so higher f means higher X<sub>L</sub>.

questions.q: If the frequency goes **up**, capacitive reactance X<sub>C</sub>…
questions.w: X<sub>C</sub> = 1 ÷ 2πfC: f is underneath, so higher f means lower X<sub>C</sub>.

questions.q: In a pure **inductor**, the current…
o: is in phase with the voltage
questions.w: Inductive = **lagging**. Lenz's law: the coil opposes the change in current.

questions.q: In a pure **capacitor**, the current…
o: is in phase with the voltage
questions.w: Capacitive = **leading**. The current flows first to put charge on the plates.

questions.q: Can **DC** flow through a capacitor (once charged)?
o: Yes, but only at high voltage
questions.w: The plates are separated by an insulator (the dielectric). DC stops once the capacitor has charged.

questions.q: A coil has **R = 30 Ω** and **X<sub>L</sub> = 40 Ω**. Find the **impedance**.
**R = 25 Ω** and **L = 0.1 H** are in series on **230 V, 50 Hz**. Find the **current**.
**R = 40 Ω**, **Z = 50 Ω**. Find the **power factor**.
**R = 30 Ω**, **L = 0.2 H** and **C = 50 μF** are in series at **50 Hz**. Find **Z**.
A load takes **5 A** from **230 V** at a power factor of **0.8**. Find the **power**.
For R, L and C in series, which formula gives the impedance?
questions.w: X<sub>L</sub> and X<sub>C</sub> act in opposite directions, so you **subtract** them.

questions.q: Power factor is the ratio of…
questions.w: PF = real power (W) ÷ apparent power (VA) = cos θ.

questions.q: In parallel: **I<sub>R</sub> = 3 A** and **I<sub>C</sub> = 4 A**. Find the **supply current**.
In parallel: **I<sub>R</sub> = 6 A**, **I<sub>L</sub> = 8 A**, **I<sub>C</sub> = 2 A**. Find the **supply current**.
**230 V** across **R = 46 Ω**, **X<sub>L</sub> = 23 Ω** and **X<sub>C</sub> = 92 Ω**, all in parallel. Find the **supply current**.
In parallel, **I<sub>R</sub> = 8 A** and **I<sub>T</sub> = 10 A**. Find the **power factor**.
In a parallel circuit, what is the **same** in every branch?
questions.w: Every branch is connected across the same supply, so the **voltage** is the same.

questions.q: Find the **time constant** for **R = 10 kΩ** and **C = 100 μF**.
A capacitor charges from **12 V**. What is its voltage after **one time constant**?
**R = 4.7 kΩ**, **C = 220 μF**. How long until it is **fully charged** (5τ)?
After **one time constant**, a charging capacitor reaches about…
questions.w: 63 % after 1τ. About 99 % (fully charged) after 5τ.

questions.q: A **star** system has a line voltage of **400 V**. Find the **phase voltage**.
A **delta** load has a phase current of **10 A**. Find the **line current**.
A **delta** load on **400 V** has **R = 16 Ω** and **X<sub>L</sub> = 12 Ω** per phase. Find the **line current**.
In a **star** connection…
questions.w: Star: the **voltages** differ by √3, the currents are the same.

questions.q: The three phases of a 3-phase supply are separated by…
Under the current colour code, the three line conductors are…
questions.w: L1 brown, L2 black, L3 grey. Neutral is blue.

questions.q: A solenoid has **500 turns**, carries **3 A** and has a flux path of **0.25 m**. Find **H**.
Air-cored: **H = 8000 At/m**. Find the flux density **B** in **millitesla**.
**B = 0.4 T** over an area of **0.005 m²**. Find the flux **Φ** in **milliwebers**.
Flux density **B** is measured in…
questions.w: 1 tesla = 1 Wb/m².

questions.q: Magnetomotive force (MMF) is…
questions.w: MMF = I × N, measured in ampere-turns (At).

questions.q: A **4-pole** alternator runs at **1500 r/min**. Find the **frequency**.
A generator makes **120 V at 25 r/s**. Flux stays the same. What EMF at **40 r/s**?
Fleming's **right-hand** rule is used for…
questions.w: **Right** hand = generators. **Left** hand = motors. Thumb = motion, first finger = field, second finger = current.

questions.q: Which three things are needed to induce an EMF?
o: A battery, a switch and a load
A conductor, a magnetic field and relative motion
A capacitor, an inductor and a resistor
A rotor, a stator and a centrifugal switch
questions.w: No movement between conductor and field = no induced EMF.

questions.q: Find the synchronous speed of a **2-pole** motor on **50 Hz**.
Synchronous speed **1000 rpm**, rotor speed **960 rpm**. Find the **slip**.
A **4-pole**, **50 Hz** motor has **5 % slip**. Find the **rotor speed**.
Synchronous speed **2000 rpm**, rotor speed **1800 rpm**. Find the **slip**.
Why does a single-phase induction motor need help to start?
o: One coil gives a pulsating field, not a rotating one
questions.w: The two counter-rotating fields cancel at standstill, so there is no starting torque.

questions.q: Fleming's **left-hand** rule is used for…
questions.w: **Left** hand = motors (the motor effect).

terms.def: The **longest side** of a right-angled triangle. It is opposite the right angle.
The side **across from** the angle θ.
The side **next to** the angle θ (not the hypotenuse).
In a right-angled triangle, **hypotenuse² = opposite² + adjacent²**.
The smooth up-and-down shape of AC. It rises to a peak at 90°, falls to zero at 180°, to a negative peak at 270° and back to zero at 360°.
The **highest** value the wave reaches. For mains it is about 325 V.
From the top of the wave to the bottom: **2 × peak**.
Root mean square. The AC value that gives the **same heating as DC**. RMS = peak × 0.707. Mains is 230 V RMS.
The average over half a cycle: **0.636 × peak**.
The number of **complete cycles per second**, measured in hertz (Hz). Mains is 50 Hz.
One complete wave, from 0° round to 360°.
How much a coil opposes a **change** in current. Measured in **henrys (H)**.
An induced EMF always makes a current whose magnetic field **opposes the change** that caused it.
An inductor's opposition to AC. **X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL**, in ohms. It rises with frequency.
How much charge a capacitor stores per volt. Measured in **farads (F)**.
The **insulating** layer between the plates of a capacitor.
A capacitor's opposition to AC. **X<sub>C</sub> = 1 ÷ 2πfC**, in ohms. It falls as frequency rises.
The **total opposition** to AC from resistance and reactance together, in ohms. Z = √(R² + X²).
**Real power ÷ apparent power** = cos θ = R ÷ Z. A PF of 1 means voltage and current are in step.
The current is **behind** the voltage. Inductive loads are lagging.
The current is **ahead of** the voltage. Capacitive loads are leading.
The angle between the voltage and the current.
An arrow showing the **size and phase** of a voltage or current. Phasor diagrams are drawn to scale.
**τ = R × C**, in seconds. After 1τ a capacitor reaches 63 % of the supply voltage; after 5τ it is fully charged.
The voltage **between two lines**. 400 V on a standard supply.
The voltage **across one load** (phase). In star, U<sub>P</sub> = U<sub>L</sub> ÷ √3 = 230 V.
Each load connects from a line to a common star point. **U<sub>L</sub> = √3 × U<sub>P</sub>**, I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>P</sub>.
Each load connects between two lines. **U<sub>L</sub> = U<sub>P</sub>**, I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × I<sub>P</sub>.
The total amount of magnetic field. Measured in **webers (Wb)**.
Flux per square metre. Measured in **tesla (T)**. Φ = B × A.
The 'push' that makes magnetic flux: **current × turns**, in ampere-turns (At).
MMF per metre of flux path: **H = I × N ÷ l**, in At/m.
The fixed link between B and H in air: **μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷**, so B = μ₀ × H.
A coil of wire wound in a tight **spiral**. Current through it makes a magnetic field.
An AC generator. A magnetic field and conductors move relative to each other to induce an EMF.
Electromotive force: the voltage **induced** or generated, in volts. E is proportional to flux × speed.
For **generators**. Thumb = motion, first finger = field, second finger = induced current.
The **stationary** part of a motor. Its coils make the rotating magnetic field.
The **rotating** part of a motor, fixed to the output shaft.
The speed of the rotating magnetic field: **N<sub>S</sub> = 60 × f ÷ pole pairs**.
How much slower the rotor turns than the field: **(N<sub>S</sub> − N<sub>R</sub>) ÷ N<sub>S</sub> × 100 %**.
Number of poles ÷ 2. A 4-pole machine has 2 pole pairs.
For **motors**. Thumb = motion (force), first finger = field, second finger = current.
**10⁻³**: one thousandth. 1 mF = 0.001 F.
**10⁻⁶**: one millionth. 1 μF = 0.000001 F.
**10³**: one thousand. 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω.
